title: Checkpoint: The New Kingdom
objective: After this level you can explain how Egypt became an empire and how Akhenaten shook it.
summary: From Hyksos rule to empire: Theban kings drove out the Hyksos, built an empire and enriched Amun, then Akhenaten’s Aten revolution came and went.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: how Egypt became an empire, and how Akhenaten shook it.
cards.body: You’ve met foreign kings, a warrior pharaoh, a hidden valley and a sun-disc revolution. Here’s the New Kingdom in one sweep.

cards.headline: The New Kingdom at a glance

events.label: Second Intermediate Period: the Hyksos rule the north
Ahmose drives out the Hyksos; the New Kingdom begins
Thutmose III reigns and wins at Megiddo
Akhenaten reigns and raises the Aten

cards.headline: One story
cards.body: Foreign rule taught Egypt a lesson. Kings from Thebes drove out the Hyksos, then built buffer zones that grew into an empire, from Nubia’s gold to the Euphrates. Victory made Amun rich at Karnak, and kings hid their tombs in a valley across the river. Then Akhenaten raised the Aten above Amun and moved to a new city, where great kings wrote to him as “brother.” His revolution did not outlast him.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: Ahmose drove out the Hyksos around 1550 BCE
Buffer zones grew into an empire
Amun grew rich; kings hid their tombs
Akhenaten’s Aten revolution did not outlast him

questions.prompt: New Kingdom recap: which of these events came first?

options.label: Thutmose III wins at Megiddo
options.rationale: That came decades after the New Kingdom began.

options.label: Akhenaten raises the Aten
options.rationale: That came later still, around 1352 BCE.

options.label: The New Kingdom ends
options.rationale: That was around 1069 BCE, last of all.

questions.explanation: Ahmose expelled the Hyksos around 1550 BCE, opening the New Kingdom.

questions.prompt: What prize drew New Kingdom Egypt deep into Nubia?

options.label: Cedar forests for shipbuilding
options.rationale: Nubia’s prize lay in its deserts.

options.label: Horses for the chariot corps
options.rationale: Horses came from the north with the Hyksos.

questions.explanation: Egypt prized gold from the Nubian deserts and ran Nubia through viceroys.

questions.prompt: Why did Akhenaten’s religious revolution vanish so fast after he died?

options.label: The court returned to Thebes and Amun was restored
Nefertiti banned the worship of the Aten
options.rationale: Nefertiti worshipped the Aten beside him.

options.label: A great flood buried the new capital
options.rationale: The city was abandoned, not flooded.

questions.explanation: About four years after his death the court went back to Thebes, Akhetaten was abandoned and Amun was restored.

questions.prompt: Hiding royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings was meant to stop robbers. How well did it work?

options.label: Perfectly: no tomb was ever entered
Poorly: virtually every tomb was emptied in ancient times
Only kings from Thebes were robbed
options.rationale: Robbery hit almost all the tombs.

options.label: Robbers only arrived in modern times
options.rationale: The tombs were emptied in antiquity.

questions.explanation: Virtually all the valley’s tombs were emptied in antiquity; Tutankhamun’s is the famous exception.

questions.prompt: Nefertiti’s bust and Tushratta’s letters were both found at the site of which New Kingdom capital?

options.label: Thebes, city of Amun
options.rationale: Both finds came from Akhenaten’s own city.

options.label: Akhetaten, Akhenaten’s city of the Aten
Heliopolis, city of the sun temple
options.rationale: That’s where Thutmose III’s obelisks first stood.

questions.explanation: Both come from Tell el-Amarna, the site of Akhetaten, Akhenaten’s capital.
